analysis.one_liner: Restores the Glass-Steagall wall separating government-insured bank deposits from securities trading.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on April 9, 2019 and died there when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal key parts of the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and bring back the Glass-Steagall separation of the 1930s, which forbade a bank that holds government-insured deposits from also underwriting or dealing in stocks, bonds, and other securities. Banks would have two years to unwind existing affiliations between their deposit-taking arms and their securities businesses, and securities-firm executives could no longer sit on bank boards. Its purpose is to stop depositors' insured money from being exposed to Wall Street trading risk, and to stop taxpayers from standing behind those bets.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers. Checking and savings accounts would be held in institutions that cannot also underwrite or trade securities, so insured deposits would no longer sit inside firms that take market risks. If a securities arm of a big bank failed, it could not directly pull down the deposit-taking bank that federal insurance backs, which is the dynamic that required large public rescues after 2008.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insured depository institutions from affiliating with firms principally engaged in underwriting, selling, or distributing stocks, bonds, notes, and other securities, and bars securities-firm officers and employees from simultaneously serving as officers or directors of insured banks, ending dual roles within 60 days. [S2] [S3]
Bars any firm issuing or selling securities from receiving deposits, including checking-style transaction accounts, so securities businesses cannot fund themselves with insured bank money. [S2] [S3]

Gives banks and bank holding companies an orderly two-year wind-down, extendable by regulators in six-month increments up to one year, with early termination allowed where regulators find undue concentration, conflicts of interest, or unsound practices, and requires each such determination to be reported to Congress. [S3]

Ratifies the Supreme Court's narrow reading of bank-securities limits in Investment Company Institute v. Camp (1971) and forbids federal banking agencies and courts from interpreting the new wall more loosely than that ruling, preventing regulators from quietly re-widening the gap. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large bank holding companies and universal banks that combine commercial banking with investment banking — the model Gramm-Leach-Bliley legalized in 1999 — would have to divest or spin off their securities affiliates within two years, giving up revenue and the diversification and scale they argue benefit customers. Some economists also warn that shunting trading into unregulated shadow institutions could create new risks outside the wall.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large universal banks and securities firms

drawbacks.text: The bill gives a hard two-year deadline (with limited regulator extensions) for unwinding conglomerates built over two decades; forced divestitures on that timeline could be disruptive to markets and to some bank customers. [S3]

A 1930s-style wall does not reach all modern risk: trading and credit have migrated to hedge funds, insurers, and other institutions outside the insured-deposit system, so the bill addresses the risk that caused the 2008-era rescues but not risk in the unregulated shadow sector, a standard critique of Glass-Steagall restoration.

Defenders of universal banking argue that diversified financial firms are more stable and that separating commercial and investment banking raises costs for customers who now get multiple services from one institution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is indirect but large: insured deposits and, in a crisis, taxpayer backstops would be insulated from securities-trading losses. The costs fall mostly on a small number of very large financial firms and their shareholders, and the transition could be disruptive if forced in two years. The bill is a blunt instrument — it does not touch shadow banking — but its design includes wind-down flexibility and anti-evasion language, so it is more carefully built than a simple statutory revival. The strongest honest objection is that Glass-Steagall alone would not prevent a future crisis centered outside the banking system.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill on April 9, 2019 with 25 original cosponsors, all Democrats. [S3]
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction; that is the only committee action in its two-year history. [S5]
Thirty House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total, out of 231 House Democrats, and no Republican did. [S4] [S3]
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died at the end of the 116th Congress. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large universal banks keep the Gramm-Leach-Bliley structure that lets insured deposits coexist with securities businesses; nothing changed for them. Depositors gained nothing from a wall they never got.

for.name: Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the original cosponsors.

for.name: 30 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats.

for.name: National and local campaign groups for bank separation
for.what_they_did: Long-running campaigns (notably after the 2008 financial crisis and its bank bailouts) pressed Congress to restore Glass-Steagall, giving the issue recurring visibility.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: The committee the bill was assigned to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year life of the Congress.

against.name: Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: As chair, controlled the committee calendar and did not advance the bill.

against.name: Universal banking and securities industries
against.role: Large bank holding companies, investment banks, and their lobbying operations
against.what_they_did: Opposed revival of the bank-securities separation that Gramm-Leach-Bliley had authorized, defending the combined banking model's revenue.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican supported the bill; it received no committee or floor votes, so no roll-call breakdown exists. [S4]

industries.industry: Universal banks and large bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill's core targets: firms combining insured deposits with securities underwriting would have to unwind those affiliations within two years and give up cross-industry revenue. Their interest in keeping the combined model runs against the bill's depositor-protection purpose. [S2] [S3]

They would lose access to insured deposits (the bill bans securities firms from maintaining transaction accounts) and to bank-board influence, and their executives could no longer hold bank posts. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Community and deposit-taking banks without securities affiliates
industries.note: The separation levels the field against conglomerate rivals whose deposit arms compete with them, and the market the bill serves is the one they already occupy. Their interest aligns with the depositor-protection goal.
